results.name: outside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets lying more than 10 beyond the [min, max] range of the examples; observed > null means the model under-generalizes far outside the example range (too interval-bound), observed < null means it over-generalizes there.
results.code:
# name: outside_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets lying more than 10 beyond the [min, max] range of the examples; observed > null means the model under-generalizes far outside the example range (too interval-bound), observed < null means it over-generalizes there.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    m = (t < lo - 10) | (t > hi + 10)
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: last_digit_match_effect
results.description: Yes-rate for targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus yes-rate for targets sharing none; observed > null means humans use surface digit similarity more than the model's ends-in-d rules predict, observed < null means less.

results.name: set_size_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (rating) on the number of examples in the set (1-4); observed less negative than null means humans tighten generalization with more examples less than the size principle in the model implies, more negative means they tighten more.
results.code:
# name: set_size_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (rating) on the number of examples in the set (1-4); observed less negative than null means humans tighten generalization with more examples less than the size principle in the model implies, more negative means they tighten more.
def test_statistic(df):
    k = (df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    kv = k - k.mean()
    den = (kv ** 2).sum()
    return float((kv * (y - y.mean())).sum() / den) if den > 0 else 0.0

results.name: distance_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (rating) on the target's absolute distance to its nearest example (per 10 units); observed more negative than null means humans show steeper similarity-based generalization gradient than the model.
results.code:
# name: distance_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (rating) on the target's absolute distance to its nearest example (per 10 units); observed more negative than null means humans show steeper similarity-based generalization gradient than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1) / 10.0
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dv = d - d.mean()
    den = (dv ** 2).sum()
    return float((dv * (y - y.mean())).sum() / den) if den > 0 else 0.0

results.name: inside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside the [min, max] span of the examples (excluding the examples themselves); observed > null means humans fill in the example span (interval-like generalization) more than the model predicts, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: inside_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside the [min, max] span of the examples (excluding the examples themselves); observed > null means humans fill in the example span (interval-like generalization) more than the model predicts, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    isex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~isex
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Difference in yes-rate between late trials (trial_index above the median) and early trials; nonzero observed vs null near 0 means humans drift in yes-bias over the session, which the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: parity_match_minus_mismatch
results.description: Among uniform-parity sets, yes-rate for parity-matching targets minus yes-rate for parity-mismatching targets; observed < null means humans weight parity less than the model (model over-relies on odd/even rules), observed > null means more.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_minus_mismatch
# description: Among uniform-parity sets, yes-rate for parity-matching targets minus yes-rate for parity-mismatching targets; observed < null means humans weight parity less than the model (model over-relies on odd/even rules), observed > null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    par = np.mod(ex, 2)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    s = np.nansum(par, axis=1)
    uniform = (s == 0) | (s == n)
    setpar = (s == n).astype(float)
    tp = np.mod(df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy(), 2)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = uniform & (tp == setpar)
    b = uniform & (tp != setpar)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: cell_response_disagreement
results.description: Mean over (set, target) cells of p_hat*(1-p_hat), where p_hat is the cell's yes-rate; observed > null means humans' yes-rates are less extreme (more graded/noisy) than the model's near-0/1 posterior predictions, observed < null means more extreme.
